extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students (U.S. patent law practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and evidentiary/rule principles governing interference suits, repeal of patents, qui tam marking actions, and infringement (particularly process infringement) under U.S. patent law. Focused on what facts, pleading, evidence, and legal tests control these types of patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interfering claims must be substantially identical
rubrics_metrics.description: The interfering claims of the two patents must be substantially identical, else there is no jurisdiction under Section 4918. The identity of the claims is the sole test of the question of the existence of an interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction of the patent may affect this question and may depend on prior art; where construction can be based on the words of the patents (with or without judicial notice of facts not stated therein) the questions may be decided on demurrer, but not otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference factual issues (priority/novelty) mirror ordinary defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions concerning which party was the first inventor and whether one party had notice or was negligent relate to lack of invention, want of novelty, and any other defense that is a defense to an ordinary patent suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If complainant's invention is older, defendant's interfering claim is void for want of novelty, and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible evidence in interference suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence may consist of documents and exhibits, proved and supplemented by depositions of witnesses; depositions may be taken in the same ways as in infringement cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deposition taken in an interference in the Patent Office between the same inventions is admissible (or not) in an interference suit according to the law of evidence governing use of depositions taken in another case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticated Patent Office or appellate decisions admissible
rubrics_metrics.description: A properly authenticated copy of the decision of the Commissioner of Patents in an interference, or of the Court of Appeals of D.C. reviewing such a decision, is admissible in evidence in an interference suit between patents involved in that interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such decisions, if not reversed, operate as admissible evidence bearing on priority and entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's decision is prima facie evidence in favor of the last granted patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If not reversed by the court, the decision of the Commissioner is prima facie evidence in favor of the patent last granted because he would not have granted it if he had not decided it entitled to priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any decision of the reviewing court is likewise prima facie evidence in favor of the patent last granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunctions available in interference suits
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary injunction can be granted in an interference suit on the ground that the equity jurisdiction to entertain bills in equity under the patent act carries all incidents of that jurisdiction, including injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle (Justice Nelson's 1863 decision) has been reaffirmed and repeated in later cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper decrees in interference cases
rubrics_metrics.description: If hearing discloses no interference, decree should dismiss the complainant's bill; if there is an interference, decree should adjudge the patent issued on the later invention void so far as it covers the interfering matter and as the parties' titles extend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the later-granted patent to be voided is that of the complainant, merely dismissing the complainant's bill may be insufficient because dismissal may mean no interference or that the complainant lacks title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for repeal of patents (fraud or mistake)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents and reissues may sometimes be obtained by fraud, or be granted by mistake; such facts may be interposed as defenses to infringement suits, but when they cannot be so interposed, they may require repeal of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a patent has been signed and sealed in the Patent Office it cannot be revoked by the President or other executive officer; relief must be sought in equity to repeal or annul such patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity jurisdiction to repeal patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity has jurisdiction to repeal letters patent for inventions obtained by fraud whenever the United States files a bill stating the facts and praying that the letters patent be annulled; same jurisdiction exists for patents issued by mistake of the kind courts of equity relieve against.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdiction does not extend to mere error of judgment in deciding debatable questions of difference of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements/practice for bills to repeal patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill to repeal a patent must be filed before the expiration of the patent and in some District Court of the United States which has jurisdiction of the owner of the patent sought to be repealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The United States acts through the U.S. District Attorney under direction of the Attorney General in bringing such suits; private citizens may prompt but cannot compel the Attorney General or a District Attorney to begin or to control such a suit. Pendency of a repeal bill does not affect progress of an infringement suit based on that patent; no injunction will issue to restrain the patentee from bringing infringement suits pending repeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qui tam (marking) actions authorized and remedy structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Qui tam actions under Section 4901 forbid certain marking acts and provide that whoever commits such acts is liable to a penalty of not less than $100 with costs; any person may sue, and one-half of the penalty goes to the plaintiff and one-half to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are statutory civil penalties recoverable in District Court where the offense was committed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three forbidden marking acts (Section 4901)
rubrics_metrics.description: The forbidden acts are: (1) Unauthorized marking upon any patented article of the name, or any imitation of the name, of the patentee; (2) Unauthorized marking upon any patented article of the word 'patent' or 'patentee', or 'letters patent', or any word of like import, with intent to imitate or counterfeit the patentee's mark or device; (3) Marking upon any unpatented article the word 'patent' or any word importing that the same is patented, for the purpose of deceiving the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute distinguishes between marking patented articles and marking unpatented articles; specific intent is required for some offenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: First two forbidden acts injurious to public and patentees
rubrics_metrics.description: The first two forbidden acts mislead persons into buying and using articles made or sold in violation of patents (injurious to public security) and are also injurious to patentees by enabling infringers to pass off infringing goods as lawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law requires patentees and authorized sellers to mark patented articles; marking a case containing patented articles may not constitute the second forbidden act if the contained articles themselves could have been marked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent to deceive required for marking unpatented articles; burden on defendant to prove innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: Intent to deceive the public is a necessary element of marking an unpatented article 'patented'; that intent must exist at the time of marking and does not exist where the marker is honestly mistaken about rights. Proof of an act adapted to deceive suffices to infer intent unless the defendant proves otherwise; burden is on defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honest belief that a particular patent covers the article can rebut intent; mere ignorance (not knowing whether patented) is insufficient. Marking accompanied by words indicating the patent had expired is not the forbidden act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking offense complete at time of illegal marking; sale not necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof that the article illegally marked was afterward sold or presented to the public is not necessary; the offense is complete when the illegal marking occurs with intent to deceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If marking was done without intent but the marked article is later used for deception, the statute is not violated. Marking in one district and offering for sale in another violates the statute in the district where marking occurred but not necessarily in the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty amount strictly construed
rubrics_metrics.description: The penalty 'not less than one hundred dollars' in the penal statute must be strictly construed and authorizes a penalty of precisely one hundred dollars and no more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Thayer instructed that several unpatented articles marked 'patented' on the same day and practically continuously may constitute only one offense and thus a single penalty for all such articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qui tam plaintiff must be a natural person suing in own name
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff in a qui tam action may be any 'person' (a natural person, not an artificial person) and must sue in his own name, not in that of the United States, although he may state he sues for the United States as well as himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plurality of persons cannot join as plaintiffs under analogous copyright precedent; the defendant may be an individual or corporation. Death of a natural person defendant will end the qui tam case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for qui tam actions vested in District Courts where act committed
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction in qui tam actions has always been conferred solely upon District Courts, for each case upon the particular District Court within whose district the forbidden act was committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuit Courts historically did not have this jurisdiction for qui tam patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and pleading requirements for qui tam actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper common-law form is debt; in code states use code forms. The declaration/complaint/petition ought to state all the elements of the forbidden act and charge that the act was contrary to the statute; each marking complained of must be separately stated to recover cumulatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to aver the uses to which the penalty will be applied. The sufficiency of pleading is tested by civil pleading rules of the state in which the District Court sits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctions to restrain repetition of marking acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons guilty of either of the first two classes of forbidden marking acts may be restrained by injunction from any repetition of such acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have granted injunctive relief to prevent further deceptive marking or counterfeit marking practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of process patents tests (substantial use of claimed process)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a process is infringed by one who, without ownership or license, uses substantially the process which the patent claims; this holds whether or not the infringer uses substantially the apparatus described, or the materials prescribed, or equivalents therefor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tilghman v. Proctor and other cases illustrate infringement can occur despite differences in proportions, temperatures, means of heating, or additions to the process if the accused process substantially includes that of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of a process step avoids infringement only if no equivalent substituted
rubrics_metrics.description: No process patent is infringed where any one of the series of acts which constitute the process is omitted by the supposed infringer unless some equivalent act is substituted for the one omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalency has been viewed as an act that works in substantially the same way to accomplish the same result (examples include tamping oil wells with benzine vs water). The Supreme Court has not precisely defined equivalency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition to a patented process does not avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: An addition to a patented process does not avert infringement of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the accused method adds useful steps or improvements, the core patented process may still be infringed (illustrated in cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests and doctrines for infringement by equivalents (function/way/result; substantial sameness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement analysis contemplates equivalents, substitution, transposition or omission of parts; tests include sameness of function, substantial sameness of way of performance, and whether substituted parts are equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues include necessity of change in equivalents, primary vs secondary inventions in applying doctrine of equivalents, and consideration of changes of form or proportion; knowledge of the patent by the infringer is not a necessary element of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of compositions: substitution and proportion changes
rubrics_metrics.description: For patents on compositions of matter, substitution of ingredients may constitute infringement when ingredients are equivalents; changes of proportion in compositions are relevant to infringement analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., Giant-Powder examples) illustrate substitution-of-ingredients disputes and the concept of equivalent vs non-equivalent ingredients; disclaimers of particular equivalents may affect scope.
